lab.name: LAB (Linear Alkylbenzene)
lab.chainNote: Benzene NWE is the 4–6 week leading indicator for LAB NWE. Naphtha provides the 2-step upstream signal. Monitoring benzene weekly gives procurement teams advance warning of LAB movements.

cyclePos.verdict: Mid-range — pulled back from 2024 peak. Index stabilising around 108 as benzene normalises. Reasonable timing for 12-month contract renewal.

lab.seasonNote: Q3 peak driven by European detergent pre-season buying. Q1 trough — historically best negotiation window. Seasonal range ±6%.
lab.volNote: Medium volatility. Benzene spikes transmit 60–70% of amplitude to LAB within 6 weeks.
lab.dyn3m: LAB NWE rose 12% from the Jan 2023 reference driven by benzene tightness following unplanned cracker shutdowns. Moeve Huelva ran at 96% utilisation — near capacity — adding supply-side pressure.

signals3m.text: Benzene NWE trending up — EU cracker maintenance season approaching; LAB follows with 4–6 week lag
Naphtha NWE flat — no upstream confirmation yet; monitor for breakout
Asian import parity — Indian LAB at 115 vs. EU 112; no material arbitrage pressure currently
India: TPIL utilisation >95% — tight domestic supply, limited spot availability
India: INR weakening — increases USD/EUR cost of Indian LAB for export buyers; currency, not feedstock, is driving part of the India increase

lab.dyn24m: LAB NWE rose 12% over 24 months in three phases: flat H1 2023; +5% step-up in H2 2023 as EU cracker issues emerged; sustained plateau at 110–112 through 2024.

signals24m.text: Q3 2023: Ineos Grangemouth cracker shutdown — benzene supply tightened; LAB +4%
Q1 2024: EU energy normalisation — partial electricity offset of +1.5%
Oct 2024: Moeve launches NextLab-R bio-based LAB at ~8% premium
2026 (expected): Reliance Jamnagar LAB expansion (India) — potential regional supply relief

roles.name: Primary cost anchor — LABS family
roles.desc: LAB is the largest single cost driver in all LABS formula variants — 36–42% weight depending on variant. First index to monitor for LABS pricing movements.

roles.name: Leading indicator — benzene downstream
roles.desc: LAB NWE is 4–6 weeks downstream from benzene. A benzene move today will appear in LABS should-cost within one contract cycle.

roles.name: Import parity reference — Asian vs. EU
roles.desc: LAB NWE vs. LAB FOB India / CFR Asia spread determines when Asian-origin LABS becomes cost-competitive in Europe.

roleExtra.formula: Cost line — LAB (38–42% weight)
roleExtra.corr: r=0.82 vs. Benzene NWE (6w lag)

lab.psNote: Moeve + Sasol control ~55% of EU LAB supply. New capacity additions unlikely before 2027. Asian import parity (~€80–120/t logistics) provides the effective ceiling.
lab.upstreamNote: Benzene NWE is the dominant leading indicator — a benzene spike today reaches your LAB contract cost in approximately one contract cycle. Naphtha provides the 2-step early warning.
lab.producersNote: Asian producers (India + China + APAC) represent ~52% of global LAB capacity. EU market is supplied by Sasol and Moeve (~45% of EU) with balance from Asian imports. In India specifically, Reliance + TPIL control ~75% of domestic supply — a near-duopoly. New capacity additions concentrated in Asia — structural overhang on EU pricing; Reliance Jamnagar expansion (~2026) is the key India capacity event to watch.

negPointers.title: ICIS subscription required — but direction is visible for free
negPointers.body: ICIS LAB NWE is subscription-only for the precise assessed price. However, weekly LAB direction is visible in ICIS free newsletters, trade press (ICIS news), and SunSirs for Chinese domestic LAB. Use these for directional evidence in negotiations — the precise number matters less than the direction.

negPointers.title: Cite benzene as the 4–6 week leading indicator
negPointers.body: Benzene NWE is freely visible via ICIS delayed data and Chemanalyst. If benzene has risen 10% in the past month, you can credibly argue that your LAB contract will face a 6–8% cost increase in the next cycle — and negotiate proactively before it arrives.

negPointers.title: Asian import parity as negotiation ceiling
negPointers.body: LAB FOB India and CFR Asia are regularly cited in trade press. The EU-Asia spread (currently ~€20–30/t in favour of EU) is visible without a subscription. If the spread narrows to near logistics cost (~€80–120/t), Asian import competition becomes a credible threat to your EU supplier.

negPointers.title: Energy cost reduction is visible in Eurostat — cite it
negPointers.body: EU industrial electricity (Eurostat) is free and shows a -5.2% decline from the Jan 2023 reference. Electricity is ~7% of LABS formula weight. You can quantify the supplier energy cost saving directly from free public data — a powerful challenge to any cost-increase claim.

negPointers.title: India: separate feedstock cost from currency in your challenge
negPointers.body: When Indian LAB prices rise, decompose it: how much is benzene (feedstock) vs. INR depreciation (currency)? If your contract is in EUR/USD, the currency effect is not a legitimate cost-pass-through — it is the supplier absorbing currency risk. Challenge currency-driven increases separately from feedstock-driven ones.

sust.name: LAB is readily biodegradable — no restriction
sust.desc: Meets OECD 301B. Compliant with EU Detergents Regulation EC 648/2004. No REACH restriction for standard grades.

sust.name: Moeve NextLab-R entering the ICIS assessment
sust.desc: Bio-based LAB launched Oct 2024. ICIS assessment does not yet separate bio-LAB pricing. As volumes grow, expect a separate bio-LAB assessment (~2026). Currently commands €80–120/t premium.

sust.name: 8–12 respondents · spot transactions only
sust.desc: ICIS NWE assessment based on reported spot transactions and bids/offers. Contract prices (majority of volume) not directly captured. Spot can diverge from contract during supply disruptions.

sust.name: HF vs. Detal alkylation — same index, different impurity profiles
sust.desc: ICIS does not distinguish between process routes. Both are included at the same price. Specification risk sits downstream — some EU formulators require Detal-origin for sustainability claims.

sust.name: India: linearity specification variability — verify COA
sust.desc: Indian LAB specification is nominally ≥90% linear but some batches from secondary producers have tested at 85–88%. Always request linearity COA for Indian-origin product, especially for EU export.

pko.name: PKO (MPOB)
pko.chainNote: PKO price is set by palm kernel crushing economics in Malaysia and Indonesia. The spread between CPO and PKO reflects the relative demand for C12–C14 vs. C16–C18 oleochemical chains. Biodiesel policy is the single biggest swing factor — when biodiesel mandates increase, CPO is diverted away from oleochemicals, tightening the oleo feedstock market.

cyclePos.verdict: At 42-month low — most favourable buying environment in the data series. Palm oil structural oversupply continuing. Lock in contracts now.

pko.seasonNote: PKO peaks Q3–Q4 as personal care demand builds ahead of year-end and Northern Hemisphere winter. Q1–Q2 trough historically offers best procurement timing.
pko.volNote: Moderate volatility. Less volatile than crude but sensitive to Indonesian biodiesel mandate changes and El Niño weather events.
pko.dyn3m: PKO softened 4.2% from the Jan 2023 reference as palm oil oversupply persists. Biodiesel sector demand for CPO has not absorbed the production surplus. The C12–C14 oleochemical demand is steady — the weakness is entirely supply-side.

signals3m.text: Palm oil production surplus — Malaysia and Indonesia running above historical average; bearish signal
Biodiesel mandate — Indonesia B35 mandate absorbing some CPO but not enough to clear surplus
CAPB / SLS demand — personal care demand stable but not growing fast enough to offset supply pressure

pko.dyn24m: PKO has declined 4.2% over 24 months — one of the few indexes in the CostAdvisor library showing a sustained downward trend. The structural driver is palm oil production expansion in Indonesia outpacing demand growth. The EUDR (EU Deforestation Regulation) from December 2024 introduces compliance cost that has not yet fully transmitted to price.

signals24m.text: 2023: Palm oil production record — PKO surplus builds; index -2%
2024: Further production growth — biodiesel absorption insufficient; index reaches low
Dec 2024: EUDR implementation — sustainability compliance cost beginning to differentiate certified vs. conventional PKO

roles.name: Primary anchor — C12–C14 oleochemical chain
roles.desc: PKO is the feedstock anchor for all C12–C14 oleochemical derivatives: fatty alcohols (lauryl, myristyl), SLS, AES, CAPB, APG, fatty amines C12–C14. The largest single cost driver for these formulas.

roles.name: CPO / PKO spread signal
roles.desc: When PKO trades at premium to CPO (typical 20–30%), C12–C14 chain products are more expensive relative to C16–C18. Buyers should monitor the spread — it signals relative feedstock cost for lauric vs. palmitic chains.

roles.name: Sustainability indicator — RSPO certification premium
roles.desc: RSPO-certified PKO trades at a premium of $30–60/t over conventional. For buyers with sustainability commitments, this premium is a real cost line that should be in the formula.

roleExtra.formula: Cost line — PKO/CPO (35–55% weight)
roleExtra.corr: r=0.91 vs. CPO (co-product)

pko.psNote: Indonesian producers supply the largest volume but carry the highest EUDR compliance risk. Malaysian producers (RSPO-certified) command a small premium and are better positioned for EU market access post-December 2024.
pko.upstreamNote: PKO and CPO move together as co-products of palm oil milling (r=0.91). The PKO/CPO spread reflects relative demand for C12–C14 vs. C16–C18 chains. Biodiesel policy is the dominant swing factor — watch Indonesian energy ministry announcements.
pko.producersNote: Indonesian producers (Sinar Mas/GAR, Musim Mas, smallholders) supply ~45% of global PKO volume but carry the highest EUDR compliance risk. Sinar Mas/GAR has had historical RSPO suspension issues — verify current certification status before specifying as a source. Malaysian producers (Wilmar, Felda, KLK, Sime Darby, IOI — mostly RSPO-certified) are better positioned for EU market access post-December 2024. KLK is unique — they both produce PKO in Malaysia and convert it to oleochemicals at KLK Emmerich (Germany).

negPointers.title: MPOB is free and public — cite it directly in every negotiation
negPointers.body: The Malaysian Palm Oil Board publishes monthly PKO prices free of charge at mpob.gov.my. This is the accepted industry benchmark. Any supplier claiming PKO cost increases must align with MPOB published data. Download the monthly PDF and attach it to your negotiation letter.

negPointers.title: PKO is at a 24-month low — challenge any price increase request
negPointers.body: The PKO MPOB index at 95.8 is near its 24-month low. If your supplier requests a price increase, ask them to show the PKO index movement that justifies it. The data does not support a cost-driven increase at current levels.

negPointers.title: RSPO premium — get certified product in your contract spec
negPointers.body: RSPO-certified PKO commands only a $30–60/t premium (~3–6% of formula cost) but protects against EUDR compliance risk and supports sustainability claims. Specify RSPO Mass Balance as a minimum in your contract — it is inexpensive insurance.

negPointers.title: Lock in now — PKO is near multi-year low
negPointers.body: Current PKO index at 18th percentile of 24-month range. Biodiesel oversupply is structural. This is a favourable buying environment — consider locking in 12-month contracts at current levels rather than remaining on spot.

sust.name: RSPO certification — premium vs. conventional
sust.desc: RSPO-certified PKO commands $30–60/t premium. For buyers with sustainability commitments or EU customers, specify RSPO Mass Balance or Segregated in your contract. Non-certified PKO faces increasing market access risk in EU from 2025.

sust.name: EU Deforestation Regulation — in force December 2024
sust.desc: EUDR requires supply chain traceability for palm oil (including PKO) sold into the EU market. Operators must prove no deforestation after December 2020. Indonesian suppliers face higher compliance burden. Compliance cost estimated at $10–25/t additional — beginning to appear in price differentials.

sust.name: ISCC certification for bio-based claims
sust.desc: ISCC (International Sustainability and Carbon Certification) is required for PKO-derived ingredients sold as bio-based under EU renewable energy or bio-economy frameworks. Increasingly specified by personal care and HI&I buyers with Scope 3 commitments.

sust.name: MPOB index — free, transparent, monthly
sust.desc: The Malaysian Palm Oil Board publishes monthly reference prices freely. No subscription required. The methodology is transparent and widely accepted as the benchmark for C12–C14 oleochemical chain pricing globally. Low data quality risk.

cpo.name: CPO (MPOB)
cpo.chainNote: CPO is the feedstock for C16–C18 oleochemical chains (palmitic, stearic, oleic fatty acids, C16–C18 fatty alcohols, FAME/biodiesel). The CPO price is set by plantation economics in Malaysia and Indonesia, with biodiesel demand as the dominant swing factor.

cyclePos.verdict: At 42-month low — strongest buyer positioning in the data series. CPO structural oversupply ongoing. Consider 12–18 month contracts to lock in current levels.

cpo.seasonNote: CPO peaks Q3–Q4 driven by biodiesel blending demand. Q1–Q2 seasonal trough. Planting cycle creates a 12–18 month lag on supply response to price signals.
cpo.volNote: Moderate-high volatility. Biodiesel mandate changes (Indonesia B35, Malaysia B20) can cause rapid ±10% moves. Weather (El Niño) affects harvest 6–9 months forward.
cpo.dyn3m: CPO softened 3.8% from the Jan 2023 reference. Indonesian B35 biodiesel mandate absorbing some production but overall supply growth outpaces demand. C16–C18 oleochemical buyers are benefiting from the weakest CPO market since 2020.

signals3m.text: Palm production surplus — Malaysian and Indonesian stocks above seasonal average
Indonesia B35 mandate — absorbing ~3.5 Mt/yr CPO equivalent; stable not growing
Soybean oil competition — US soy crop improving; limits CPO upside

cpo.dyn24m: CPO declined 3.8% over 24 months — palm oil entered a structural oversupply phase following the 2021–22 spike. Plantation expansion from 2016–2020 is now flowing through as increased production. EUDR implementation cost is the one potential price support.

signals24m.text: 2022–23: Post-Ukraine spike correction — CPO fell from record $1,600/t; base 100 set at normalised level
2023–24: Production growth absorbs demand — index drifts to 96.2
2024: EUDR introduces compliance cost — beginning to show in certified vs. conventional spread

roles.name: Primary anchor — C16–C18 oleochemical chain
roles.desc: CPO is the feedstock for palmitic (C16) and stearic/oleic (C18) fatty acid and alcohol chains. Used in fatty acids, alkyd resins, RBD palm oil, and FAME/biodiesel formulas.

roles.name: Biodiesel demand barometer
roles.desc: CPO price movements are dominated by biodiesel policy. Monitoring Indonesian and Malaysian biodiesel mandates is essential for CPO price forecasting.

roleExtra.formula: Cost line — CPO (52–62% weight)
roleExtra.corr: r=0.91 vs. PKO (co-product)

cpo.psNote: Indonesian producers dominate volume but Malaysian producers command sustainability premium. EUDR compliance cost is beginning to create a two-tier market.
cpo.upstreamNote: CPO is primarily demand-driven by biodiesel mandates (Indonesia B35 = ~3.5 Mt/yr diversion). Production expansion in Indonesia is the structural supply driver. El Niño weather events are the main upside risk to supply.
cpo.producersNote: Indonesia dominates CPO production volume but Malaysian producers are generally better-positioned on sustainability compliance (RSPO, EUDR). Watch Indonesian energy ministry announcements on biodiesel mandates — B40 introduction would be significantly bullish for CPO.

negPointers.title: MPOB is free — the most transparent commodity benchmark available
negPointers.body: MPOB monthly CPO price is published free at mpob.gov.my. It is the globally accepted C16–C18 oleochemical feedstock reference. Unlike ICIS subscriptions, any stakeholder can verify the number. Attach the MPOB PDF to your negotiation correspondence.

negPointers.title: Monitor Indonesian biodiesel mandate — the single biggest CPO swing factor
negPointers.body: Indonesia B35 mandate diverts ~3.5 Mt/yr CPO. If Indonesia raises to B40 (mooted), that is another ~2 Mt/yr diversion from oleochemicals — a significant bullish catalyst. Monitor Indonesian energy ministry announcements at esdm.go.id.

negPointers.title: CPO near 24-month low — challenge any supplier cost-increase narrative
negPointers.body: CPO index at 22nd percentile. The MPOB data does not support a feedstock-driven cost increase claim from suppliers at current levels. Use the freely available monthly data series to construct your challenge.

sust.name: RSPO certification increasingly required for EU market
sust.desc: Same as PKO — RSPO certification required for EU buyers post-EUDR. Mass Balance and Segregated supply chains command premium. Specify in contracts.

sust.name: EU Deforestation Regulation — deforestation-free proof required
sust.desc: CPO is a Category 1 commodity under EUDR. All operators placing CPO-derived products on the EU market must provide geolocation data proving no deforestation after Dec 2020. Indonesian compliance is lagging — Malaysian suppliers better positioned.

sust.name: Biodiesel mandate drives price — track Indonesian policy
sust.desc: Indonesia B35 mandate diverts ~3.5 Mt/yr CPO from oleochemical market. Policy changes (B40 mooted) would be the single largest bullish catalyst for CPO. Monitor Indonesian energy ministry announcements.

sust.name: MPOB index — free, transparent, monthly
sust.desc: Free monthly price published by Malaysian Palm Oil Board. Widely accepted benchmark. No subscription required.

electricity.name: Industrial Electricity
electricity.chainNote: EU: TTF gas sets marginal price — 1–2 quarter leading indicator. CN: NDRC regulated tariff — policy decision not market. NA: EIA state-level data — Henry Hub gas is the upstream driver. IN: CERC quarterly — rising with industrial growth. MEA: IEA proxy — subsidised, understates true cost advantage.

chain.s:
Wind · solar · hydro
Zero marginal cost

cyclePos.verdict: EU at 42-month low. NA similarly low. CN and IN diverge — CN declining on regulatory reform, IN rising with industrial growth. MEA structurally suppressed by subsidies. See regional selector for specific cycle position.

electricity.seasonNote: EU/NA: winter peak (heating demand). CN/IN: more uniform — tariff-driven with minimal seasonality. MEA: summer peak (cooling demand). Seasonal range ±3–5% for market-priced regions.
electricity.volNote: High volatility for market-priced regions (EU, NA) — driven by gas prices which had extreme moves in 2022–23. Regulated regions (CN, IN, MEA) very low volatility — policy risk not market risk.
electricity.dyn3m: EU electricity at 90.2 — down 9.8% from Jan 2023 reference as 2022 energy crisis fully unwinds. NA at 91.0 — similar trend. CN at 96.0 — modest NDRC-driven decline. India at 99.8 — essentially flat, rising industrial tariffs offsetting efficiency. MEA at 98.8 — subsidised and stable.

signals3m.text: TTF gas (EU) — stable to soft; EU storage above seasonal average; no near-term pressure
Henry Hub (NA) — US gas structurally cheap; EIA electricity costs continuing to moderate
NDRC (CN) — tariff stable; renewable reform may bring step-change reduction by 2026
CERC (IN) — Indian industrial electricity rising with capacity constraints; watch state-level variation

electricity.dyn24m: The 42-month period reveals structural divergence between regions. EU and NA fell ~10% as 2022 energy crisis unwound and renewables expanded. China declined ~4% via regulated tariff adjustments. India rose modestly as industrial demand growth strained grid capacity. MEA remained near base — subsidised and insulated from market dynamics.

signals24m.text: 2022–23: EU energy crisis peak — electricity at 118, now fully reversed to 90.2
2024–25: Renewables reach 47% of EU generation — structural downward pressure confirmed
CN 2025–26: NDRC tariff reform discussion — potential step-change reduction
IN 2025–26: CERC tariff adjustments reflect industrial growth — small upward trend

electricity.upstreamNote: Market-priced regions (EU, NA): gas price is the 1–2 quarter leading indicator. Regulated regions (CN, IN, MEA): policy decisions — watch government announcements, not market prices. Renewable expansion is the structural long-term bearish driver for EU and NA.

supply.t: CN grid · 60% coal · renewable growing fast

electricity.producersNote: EU and NA have competitive electricity markets — multiple generators compete. CN, IN, and MEA are state-monopoly regulated systems. For formula purposes: EU/NA respond to market dynamics; CN/IN/MEA respond to policy decisions. MEA formula systematically understates actual supplier energy cost advantage due to subsidies.

negPointers.title: EU Eurostat is free — cite it directly in every negotiation
negPointers.body: EU industrial electricity prices are published free quarterly by Eurostat at ec.europa.eu/eurostat. At 90.2 vs. a Jan 2023 base of 100, EU electricity is 9.8% BELOW the reference. Any supplier still applying 2022-era energy surcharges has no data support for it.

negPointers.title: TTF gas is the 1–2 quarter EU leading indicator — monitor freely
negPointers.body: TTF gas spot price is freely available with 15-minute delay via ICE. A TTF decline today predicts EU electricity tariff reduction in 1–2 quarters. Use this to pre-empt supplier cost narratives.

negPointers.title: Ask for the actual provincial tariff — Xinjiang is 30–40% below Shandong
negPointers.body: CEIC Shandong is the default but Chinese electricity varies enormously by province. Xinjiang and Inner Mongolia (major renewable provinces) have industrial tariffs 30–40% below Shandong. Ask your Chinese supplier which province they operate in.

negPointers.title: India electricity rising — verify CERC tariff for your supplier state
negPointers.body: Indian industrial electricity is rising modestly but varies significantly by state. CERC publishes tariffs free. If your Indian supplier claims energy cost increases, request the state-level tariff documentation.

negPointers.title: MEA energy cost is structurally understated in the formula
negPointers.body: MEA industrial electricity is subsidised — published IEA proxy prices significantly understate the actual competitive advantage of MEA-based production. When comparing EU vs. MEA supplier costs, the formula electricity line should be adjusted downward for MEA origin.

roleExtra.formula: Cost line — Electricity (7–52% weight)
roleExtra.corr: r=0.78 vs TTF gas (EU) · regulated elsewhere

roles.name: Universal cost line — present in all 36 formulas across all regions
roles.desc: Industrial electricity appears in every formula in the CostAdvisor library as an energy cost line, typically at 7–52% weight. The most widely-used index in the system.

roles.name: Free data (EU, NA, IN) — maximum negotiation transparency
roles.desc: Eurostat (EU), EIA (NA), and CERC (IN) all publish industrial electricity prices free of charge. This makes electricity one of the most powerful negotiation levers — you can cite the exact tariff data your supplier uses without paying for it.

roles.name: Regulated vs. market — fundamentally different risk profiles
roles.desc: EU and NA electricity responds to market dynamics (TTF gas, renewable build-out). CN, IN, MEA electricity responds to policy decisions. These require different monitoring strategies — gas price for EU, government announcements for CN/IN/MEA.

sust.name: EU electricity 47% renewable in 2024 — Scope 2 claims possible
sust.desc: EU industrial buyers can purchase Guarantees of Origin (GOs) to claim renewable electricity. GO premium is only €1–3/MWh. Increasingly required for Scope 2 carbon accounting under GHG Protocol and CSRD.

sust.name: CN and IN grids are coal-dominant — significant Scope 2 emissions
sust.desc: Shandong grid is ~60% coal (emission factor ~750–850 gCO₂/kWh vs. EU ~250–300). Indian grids are similarly coal-heavy. Chinese and Indian chemical buyers with Scope 2 targets face a structural challenge — renewable PPAs are the primary mitigation route.

sust.name: MEA electricity subsidised — formula understates structural advantage
sust.desc: MEA industrial electricity is subsidised by Gulf state governments. Published IEA proxy prices understate the actual cost advantage by an estimated 30–50%. When comparing MEA vs. EU supplier costs, adjust the electricity line in Portfolio to reflect actual energy cost advantage.

sust.name: Eurostat is average — your actual tariff may differ
sust.desc: Eurostat publishes average EU industrial tariffs by consumption band. Your actual tariff depends on your consumption volume, grid connection voltage, country, and any renewable PPAs in place. Use actual energy contract tariff in Portfolio for precise formula calibration.

elec-eu.name: EU Industrial Electricity
elec-eu.chainNote: EU industrial electricity price is set by the intersection of gas-fired power plant economics (TTF gas), renewable energy penetration (wind and solar), and the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) carbon price. TTF is the dominant short-term driver — a TTF spike transmits to industrial electricity within 1–2 quarters.

cyclePos.verdict: At 42-month low and continuing to decline. EU electricity fell ~10% from Jan 2023 reference. Structural renewable build-out is the driver — trend expected to continue.

elec-eu.seasonNote: Winter peak (Q1, Q4) driven by heating demand. Summer trough as renewables peak and industrial demand eases. Less pronounced than gas due to grid diversification.
elec-eu.volNote: High volatility — driven by TTF gas which had extreme moves in 2022–23. Structural renewable build-out should reduce volatility over time but near-term gas dependence remains.
elec-eu.dyn3m: EU industrial electricity declined 5.2% from the Jan 2023 reference as TTF gas prices normalised from the 2022 crisis peak. Renewable capacity additions (wind + solar) provided further offset. The index at 94.8 is below the Jan 2023 reference for the first time since the energy crisis began.

signals3m.text: TTF gas stable-to-soft — EU storage levels above seasonal average; no near-term supply stress
Renewable capacity additions — EU solar installations running at record pace; structural offset to gas costs
ETS carbon price — stable at €60–65/t; not a near-term driver

elec-eu.dyn24m: EU electricity index declined 5.2% over 24 months as the 2022 energy crisis (when the index briefly reached 118) unwound. The structural story is favourable — renewable build-out is reducing gas dependence. The index is now below the Jan 2023 reference, which itself was an elevated post-crisis level.

signals24m.text: 2023 H1: TTF normalisation begins — electricity index -3%
2023–2024: Renewable additions accelerate; index continues to decline
2024: Index reaches below-reference level for first time post-crisis

roles.name: Universal cost line — present in all 22 EU formulas
roles.desc: Electricity appears in every EU formula as an energy cost line, typically at 7–22% weight. It is the most widely used index in the CostAdvisor EU formula universe.

roles.name: Free data — no subscription required
roles.desc: Eurostat publishes quarterly industrial electricity prices by country and sector free of charge. Country-level breakdown available (DE, FR, ES, NL etc.) for more granular analysis.

roles.name: Quarterly lag — forward-looking signal
roles.desc: The Eurostat index is published quarterly with 1-quarter lag. For near-term signals, TTF gas spot price is a 1–2 quarter leading indicator for EU industrial electricity.

roleExtra.formula: Cost line — Electricity (7–22% weight)
roleExtra.corr: r=0.78 vs. TTF gas (1Q lag)

elec-eu.psNote: Gas-fired plants set the marginal price most hours in most EU markets. Renewable additions are steadily reducing gas price-setting hours — structurally bearish for industrial electricity over 3–5 year horizon.
elec-eu.upstreamNote: TTF gas is the dominant 1–2 quarter leading indicator for EU industrial electricity. Gas-fired plants set the marginal price in most EU markets most hours. Renewable capacity additions are the structural counter-force — watch ENTSO-E capacity data for the long-term trajectory.

supply.t: <10% · historic low · solar overtook coal in 2024

elec-eu.producersNote: Renewables reached 47% of EU electricity in 2024 — a milestone. Nuclear (24%) and gas (16%) are the other major sources. Gas still sets the marginal price in many market hours, but solar and wind periods of near-zero marginal cost are increasingly frequent. Structurally bearish for industrial electricity costs: coal below 10% for first time ever, gas declining for 5th consecutive year.

negPointers.title: Eurostat is free — and your supplier knows you can see it
negPointers.body: EU industrial electricity prices are published free by Eurostat quarterly. Any supplier claiming energy cost increases must align with the Eurostat data series. The quarterly lag is known — use the most recent quarter as your evidence. Download at ec.europa.eu/eurostat.

negPointers.title: EU electricity index is below the Jan 2023 reference — challenge energy surcharges
negPointers.body: The Eurostat EU industrial electricity index at 94.8 is BELOW base 100. If your LABS or PAM supplier is still applying energy surcharges from the 2022 crisis, the Eurostat data directly contradicts the justification. Energy costs have normalised.

negPointers.title: TTF gas is the 1–2 quarter leading indicator — monitor freely
negPointers.body: TTF gas spot price is freely available with 15-minute delay via ICE. A TTF decline today predicts an EU electricity tariff reduction in 1–2 quarters. Use this to anticipate your supplier cost structure before they do — and pre-empt their narrative.

negPointers.title: Request Guarantees of Origin for Scope 2 accounting
negPointers.body: EU industrial buyers can purchase Guarantees of Origin (GOs) to claim renewable electricity. The GO premium is only €1–3/MWh — negligible. If your supplier is charging a green energy premium above €5/MWh, challenge the margin they are taking on the GO mechanism.

sust.name: EU electricity grid decarbonising — green power claims possible
sust.desc: EU industrial buyers can purchase Guarantees of Origin (GOs) to claim renewable electricity. GO premium currently €1–3/MWh — negligible relative to total electricity cost. Increasingly required for Scope 2 carbon accounting.

sust.name: EU ETS carbon price embedded in electricity cost
sust.desc: Carbon cost of gas-fired generation is embedded in the Eurostat index. ETS price of €60–65/t adds approximately €12–15/MWh to gas generation cost. This cost disappears if renewable share grows. Track ETS price as a leading indicator for electricity cost trajectory.

sust.name: Eurostat survey — country average, may not reflect your tariff
sust.desc: Eurostat publishes average industrial tariffs across consumption bands. Your actual tariff depends on your consumption band, grid connection, and country. For precise formula calibration, use your actual energy contract tariff as the Portfolio input.

elec-cn.name: China Industrial Electricity
elec-cn.chainNote: Chinese industrial electricity is set by NDRC regulated tariffs, which are adjusted infrequently and reflect a blend of coal, hydro, and growing renewable capacity. Shandong province is the default for Chinese chemical industry as it hosts the largest concentration of PAM, iron salt, and specialty chemical production.

regLabels.CN: CN — NBS urban unit average wage (manufacturing)
regLabels.LA: LA — Brazil IBGE (government statistics office; free)

lci-na.chainNote: The Labour Cost Index is the fixed-cost escalator used in every formula in this library — it represents the labour and overhead cost component that does not track commodity prices. It is the most universally applied index in the library (255 formulas), but also the one buyers have the least direct negotiating leverage over, since it reflects broad economy-wide wage trends rather than a specific commodity market. NA uses the BLS Employment Cost Index (ECIALLCIV, quarterly); EU uses Eurostat LCI for industry (lc_lci_r2_q, quarterly) — both are genuine pulled/tracked official series. CN, IN, MEA, LA and APAC were added as CONSTRUCTED series: a smooth monthly path built from published annual/quarterly growth rates (not a directly pulled official monthly index). CN uses NBS China urban-unit manufacturing wage growth (~4%/yr); IN uses Labour Bureau CPI-IW growth as a proxy for wage inflation (~7%/yr, the official Wage Rate Index base 2016=100 exists but was not machine-readable at build time); LA uses Brazil IBGE (government statistics office) labour cost index and real wage growth as a stand-in for the whole region; MEA blends WTW's Africa salary-budget survey with Gulf salary guides and is the weakest/most heterogeneous of the six (Gulf nominal growth ~2-4% vs. Africa ~6-7%, one series even showed a YoY decline in Saudi wages); APAC (ex-China/India) uses a generic ASEAN manufacturing wage growth range with no country-specific sourcing. Treat CN/IN/LA as reasonable, MEA/APAC as rough.

cyclePos.verdict: The LCI is structurally upward-trending — it never meaningfully reverses. The current level is the highest in the 42-month window, simply because labour costs compound forward. This is a different characteristic from commodity indexes: the question is not "are labour costs at a cyclical peak" but "is the rate of increase accelerating or decelerating." EU industry LCI growth was +3.2% year-on-year in Q1 2026 (Eurostat). NA ECI growth was approximately +4% annualised in the most recent available quarter (BLS). CN/IN/LA run hotter (~4-8%/yr); MEA/APAC are rough blended estimates.

lci-na.seasonNote: No meaningful seasonality — labour costs trend upward gradually and do not follow a cyclical commodity pattern. The stepped appearance in the sparkline is expected, reflecting quarterly publication frequency.
lci-na.volNote: Extremely low volatility by design — labour costs are structurally sticky and change at macroeconomic, not commodity, timescales. This is the most stable index in the library.
lci-na.dyn3m: Labour costs are continuing their steady upward trend. EU industry LCI: +3.2% YoY in Q1 2026; NA ECI: approximately +4% annualised. Neither region is showing signs of deceleration. CN/IN continue running hotter (~4% and ~7%/yr respectively); MEA and APAC figures are rough blended estimates, not directly sourced series.

urea.name: Urea (E. Europe prill, FOB Middle East)

regLabels.multi: Global — E. Europe prill, FOB Middle East (World Bank Pink Sheet)

urea.chainNote: Urea is the world's most widely used nitrogen fertiliser and a key raw material for melamine, urea-formaldehyde resins, and specialty chemical formulations. Its price is driven primarily by natural gas cost (ammonia feedstock) and by Middle East export economics. The 2026 Iran war severely disrupted urea supply: Middle East urea exports (Strait of Hormuz) were strangled, and the IEA noted a global fertiliser security crisis. The March 2026 Pink Sheet recorded $725.6/mt — among the highest prices in years.

cyclePos.verdict: Near the top of the 42-month range — the March 2026 spike to $725.6/mt is the highest level in this window and is directly attributable to the 2026 Iran war strangling Middle East urea exports. Pre-war level was ~$385–415/mt. The Strait of Hormuz unwind may ease prices in coming months, but the fertiliser season timing adds demand-side support.

urea.seasonNote: Mild seasonal pattern driven by Northern Hemisphere spring planting season (peak demand Mar–Jun) and Southern Hemisphere equivalent. The war spike overwhelms any seasonal signal in 2026.

urea.dyn3m: Urea spiked sharply in Q1 2026 driven by Iran war disruption of Middle East export flows. The January Pink Sheet recorded $415/mt, February $472/mt, March $726/mt — a near-doubling in three months. The US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on 17 June 2026 to formally end the conflict, and CENTCOM lifted its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz the following day. Shipping traffic is recovering but remained below pre-war levels as of early July; one widely-cited trading-desk estimate expects flows to approach pre-war levels by the end of Q3 2026, roughly 3 months out from the ceasefire. Treat current elevated pricing as a wind-down, not a new baseline — but note the June 17 memorandum still requires 60 days to formalize and has been contested before.

The +40% move since Jan 2023 (reaching $3,142–3,373/mt in Q1 2026) is partly Iran war-driven (energy price spike feeding into smelting costs) and partly structural demand growth from energy transition (EV batteries, solar, grid infrastructure).

Unlike Brent or Urea, the aluminum price increase is not purely a war premium — significant structural demand uplift is also present.

zinc.chainNote: LME zinc is relevant to this library primarily through zinc oxide (used in rubber vulcanisation, some ceramic coatings, and specialty chemical applications) and zinc chloride (used as a flux in certain chemical processes). Zinc price is driven by mine supply (concentrated in China, Australia, Peru, India) and galvanising demand (steel corrosion protection). Unlike aluminum, zinc has not shown a strong energy transition demand uplift and has been broadly range-bound over the 42-month window.

cyclePos.verdict: Mid-range, broadly flat vs the Jan 2023 base. Zinc has been the most range-bound major metal in this library over the window — no sustained trend up or down. This is consistent with a market in approximate supply/demand balance with no major structural demand catalyst or supply shock.

zinc.seasonNote: Mild seasonality — galvanising demand (the largest end use) tracks construction and manufacturing cycles with a slight H2 weighting.
zinc.volNote: Lower volatility than aluminum or copper — zinc is less exposed to energy transition demand and less politically sensitive. The range within the 42-month window (roughly 76–101 base-100) is relatively contained.
zinc.dyn3m: Zinc rose through Q4 2025–Q1 2026, reaching $3,182–3,324/mt. The move is modest compared to aluminum and appears partly war-adjacent (energy cost to smelting) but primarily reflects improving galvanising demand.

Broadly range-bound vs Jan 2023 base — buyers have limited leverage but also limited pressure; good time for contract renewal at current levels

zinc.dyn24m: Zinc fell from ~$3,300/mt in Jan 2023 to lows of ~$2,390/mt by mid-2023, then gradually recovered. Q1 2026 is back near the Jan 2023 starting level — a roughly flat 42-month period with significant interim volatility.

signals24m.text: Mid-2023: Sharp selloff to ~$2,400/mt — mining supply surge + demand softening
2024–25: Gradual recovery as galvanising demand firmed
Q1 2026: Near Jan 2023 starting level — full round trip

methanol-na.name: Methanol — NA (Methanex)
methanol-na.chainNote: Methanex is the world's largest methanol producer and posts regional contract prices freely each month — one of the most valuable free commodity price sources in this library. The Iran war caused the most dramatic methanol price spike of any commodity tracked here: from ~$850/MT in Jan 2026 to $1,480/MT in Apr/May 2026 (+74% in 3 months), confirmed directly from Methanex PDF postings. The mechanism: methanol is produced from natural gas (via syngas); the war disrupted Middle East gas supply chains, European TTF spiked, and Methanex's own Trinidad and Egypt plants faced logistics disruption. The 2023-2025 monthly values in this card are estimated from known public context; the 2026 values are real Methanex posted prices.

chain.l: Formaldehyde · MTBE · acetic acid · SLES/surfactant chain

cyclePos.verdict: At the all-time high within the 42-month window — and by a very wide margin. Methanol has posted the largest absolute percentage gain of any commodity in this library. The pre-war level was ~$600-620/MT in late 2025; the current posting of $1,480/MT embeds an extraordinary war premium. If gas prices and logistics normalise, a significant retracement is plausible — but the full round-trip to pre-war levels is not guaranteed if Iranian supply stays constrained.

methanol-na.seasonNote: Mild seasonality tied to natural gas cost cycles (winter peaks) and downstream demand patterns. The war spike overwhelms any seasonal signal in 2026.
methanol-na.volNote: Extremely high volatility — the highest of any commodity in this library. Methanol price can move 50-100%+ in a single quarter when gas feedstock costs are disrupted.
methanol-na.dyn3m: The most dramatic 3-month move in the entire library: Jan 2026 ($850/MT) → Feb 2026 ($941) → Mar 2026 ($1,247) → Apr/May 2026 ($1,480). All four values are real Methanex posted prices, directly citeable. Multiple regions followed — Asia Pacific $740/MT, China $610/MT (also dramatically elevated vs Dec 2025 levels of ~$340-365/MT).

signals3m.text: 2026 Iran war: +74% in 3 months — Jan $850 → May $1,480 (Methanex posted, real data)
Asia Pacific also spiked: $365 → $740/MT — war disrupted global methanol supply chains, not just NA
Jul 2026 NA still posted at $1,480/MT — no price relief yet despite Brent unwind; gas logistics constraints persist

methanol-na.dyn24m: Methanol declined from ~$500/MT in Jan 2023 to a trough of ~$350/MT by mid-2023, then gradually recovered to ~$600-620/MT by late 2025 — a normal gas-price-following trajectory. The Iran war shock in March 2026 doubled the price in a single quarter.

signals24m.text: 2023: Decline from gas-crisis-elevated levels to ~$350/MT floor
2024-25: Gradual recovery to $600-620/MT as gas prices normalised then retraced
Mar-May 2026: Iran war — most dramatic move in this library, +74% in 3 months

methanol-na.upstreamNote: Methanol cash cost is 50-70% natural gas. The Methanex NA price closely tracks Henry Hub with a 1-2 month lag; EU contract price tracks TTF. The extraordinary 2026 war spike reflects both gas cost and supply chain logistics disruption from Hormuz closure.
methanol-na.producersNote: Methanex is by far the most useful price reference for buyers because they publish freely. Iran's production (~5% globally) was disrupted by the war; China's coal-based production is less gas-price-sensitive but faces coal cost pressure.

negPointers.body: The Methanex posted price ($1,480/MT NA, $740/MT APAC in May 2026) is publicly posted on Methanex.com and directly citable. However, at nearly 3x the pre-war base price, it embeds a large war premium. Ask suppliers whether they are sourcing at the posted price or spot, and what their actual contracted supply cost is.

negPointers.body: Methanex posts NA, EU (€/MT), Asia Pacific ($/MT), and China ($/MT) on the same page. The spread between them tells a story: APAC ($740) is substantially below NA ($1,480) in the current posting, suggesting supply routing is responding to the disruption. A buyer with APAC-origin supply has a meaningfully different cost picture.

copper.name: Copper (LME)

regLabels.multi: Global — LME copper (World Bank Pink Sheet, $/mt)

copper.chainNote: LME copper is the global benchmark for primary copper pricing, relevant to this library through copper sulfate (algicide, fungicide, micronutrient), copper oxide (catalyst), and copper-bearing specialty chemical applications. Copper has risen significantly since 2023 (+36%) driven by energy transition demand (EV wiring, grid expansion, renewable energy) compounded by war-related energy cost increases to smelting in Q4 2025–Q1 2026. Unlike aluminum, copper also benefits from concentrated supply (Chile, Congo) that creates genuine supply-side scarcity risk.

cyclePos.verdict: Near the top of the 42-month range. Copper peaked in Q1 2026 ($12,831-13,012/mt quarterly) and has begun to edge back slightly. The structural demand story (energy transition) is durable; the war energy premium to smelting is partially transient. Both support continued elevated pricing vs. 2023.

copper.seasonNote: Mild seasonality — copper demand follows industrial production and construction cycles. Secondary to structural demand trends in the current window.
copper.volNote: Moderate volatility — lower than energy or agricultural commodities because copper inventory levels (LME warehouse stocks) provide some price buffering. Structural demand trend has also provided price floor support.
copper.dyn3m: Copper held near its Q1 2026 peak of $12,500-13,000/mt, supported by energy transition demand and mining supply constraints. The war added a smelting energy cost layer but copper's move predates the Iran war.

signals3m.text: Structural demand (EV/solar/grid) is the primary driver — copper move predates the 2026 Iran war
Smelting energy cost also elevated — war-related energy price spike added cost pressure on top of demand-driven floor

copper.dyn24m: Copper rose from ~$9,200/mt in Jan 2023 to $12,529-13,012/mt in Q1 2026 — a sustained multi-year appreciation driven by energy transition demand. Q2 2024 saw a brief speculative spike above $10,000 that partially reversed before the more sustained Q4 2025 rise.

signals24m.text: 2023-24: Gradual rise from $8,500-9,200 to $9,500-10,000 range
Q4 2025: Step-up acceleration to $11,000+ as energy transition investment accelerated
Q1 2026: Peak at $12,529-13,012/mt — war energy cost + structural demand

copper.psNote: Copper supply is concentrated in Chile (~28% of global mine supply) and the DRC (~10%). Both have faced operational and political risk in recent years. Demand is increasingly dominated by energy transition themes (EV, solar, grid).
copper.upstreamNote: Copper is often described as the "metal of electrification" — the energy transition demand story is structural, not cyclical, and distinguishes copper from zinc in this library.
copper.producersNote: Copper market is oligopolistic on the mine supply side (top 10 producers ~55% of output) but more fragmented in refining. Codelco is the most influential single actor.

negPointers.title: Separate the structural from the transient in copper cost arguments
negPointers.body: A supplier citing copper cost increases since 2023 is partially correct — the structural energy-transition demand component is real and unlikely to fully reverse. However, the Q1 2026 peak ($12,500-13,000/mt) includes war-related energy smelting cost. Ask them to break down which driver they are pricing in.

negPointers.title: Cross-check against Industrial Electricity for smelting cost component
negPointers.body: Copper smelting is energy-intensive. If electricity costs in the relevant region have eased (check the Industrial Electricity card), but the supplier is still citing energy smelting cost pressure, that gap is worth probing.

iron-ore.name: Iron Ore (CFR China 62% Fe)

regLabels.multi: Global — CFR China 62% Fe (World Bank Pink Sheet, $/dmt)

iron-ore.chainNote: Iron ore (CFR China 62% Fe) is the global reference price for iron ore as a raw material. In this library it matters as a cross-check against the Iron Scrap proxy card — both are upstream inputs to iron-derived coagulants (ferric chloride, ferric sulfate) and iron oxide pigments. Iron ore has been declining since 2023 as China's steel demand growth has disappointed market expectations, providing structural downward pressure on ferrous raw material costs independent of the Iran war.

cyclePos.verdict: Near the lower end of the 42-month range. Iron ore has been in a sustained structural decline driven by softening Chinese steel demand — one of the clearest bearish commodity signals in this library. No meaningful Iran war premium, since iron ore supply routes (Australia, Brazil) are entirely separate from the Hormuz corridor.

iron-ore.seasonNote: Mild seasonality tied to Chinese steel production and construction activity cycles. The structural decline dominates over any seasonal pattern.
iron-ore.volNote: Moderate-low volatility among commodities in this library — iron ore's wide supply base (Australia, Brazil) and large inventory buffers limit short-term price spikes.
iron-ore.dyn3m: Iron ore has stabilised around $98-106/dmt in Q1 2026, roughly flat vs. the 2025 annual average. No Iran war effect — supply routes entirely bypass Hormuz.

2025-26: Partial stabilisation — Chinese infrastructure stimulus providing some floor

mop.name: Potassium Chloride / MOP

regLabels.multi: Global — MOP granular CFR Brazil (World Bank Pink Sheet, $/mt)

mop.chainNote: Muriate of Potash (MOP, potassium chloride) is the third primary plant macronutrient alongside nitrogen (urea/ammonia) and phosphate (DAP). This card completes the NPK fertiliser triangle in this library. MOP prices crashed by nearly 40% from Jan 2023 highs as sanctions on Russian and Belarusian producers (which controlled ~40% of global supply pre-2022) were partially worked around, and Canadian and German producers expanded output. The result is one of the clearest bearish supply stories in this library.

cyclePos.verdict: Well below the Jan 2023 baseline — MOP and Zinc are the two clearest structurally bearish indexes in this library. Current Q1 2026 levels ($366-381/mt) are well below the 2023 annual average ($383/mt) despite modest recent recovery. No meaningful Iran war premium — potash supply routes (Canada, North Sea) entirely bypass Hormuz.

mop.seasonNote: Mild seasonal demand pattern tied to Northern Hemisphere spring planting season (Q1-Q2 buying) similar to other fertilisers.
mop.volNote: Moderate volatility — MOP had an extreme period in 2022 (sanctions on Russia/Belarus caused prices to spike to $900+/mt) that unwound sharply through 2023. The current window only captures the tail of that unwind.
mop.dyn3m: MOP has been recovering modestly through Q1 2026 ($366-381/mt) after a prolonged decline, but remains well below the Jan 2023 base. Q1 2026 levels are slightly above the 2024 lows, suggesting a possible trough has been found.

signals3m.text: Modest recent recovery $366→$381/mt (Q1 2026) — possible floor formation after prolonged decline
No Iran war exposure — Canadian/German supply bypasses Hormuz entirely

mop.dyn24m: MOP fell from ~$500/mt in Jan 2023 to a trough near $285/mt by early 2024 as the post-sanctions supply disruption was worked around, then recovered to $290-380/mt range through 2025.

signals24m.text: 2023: Sharp decline from $500 to $330/mt as Russian/Belarusian workarounds emerged
2024: Floor around $285-300/mt — structural supply surplus from Canada + Germany
2025-26: Modest recovery to $350-380/mt — demand growth absorbing oversupply

soybean-oil.name: Soybean Oil

regLabels.multi: Global — Soybean Oil FOB US Gulf (IMF/FRED PSOILUSDM, $/mt)

soybean-oil.chainNote: Soybean oil is the world's second most widely consumed vegetable oil (after palm oil) and a key input for fatty acid derivatives, surface-active agents, and biodiesel. Unlike Corn and Wheat in this library which have fallen since 2023, Soybean Oil has risen +17% driven by strong biodiesel/bioenergy demand — this is a structurally different driver from the food/feed demand cycle that typically dominates grain prices. The Iran war had limited direct effect on soybean oil pricing (US and Brazilian supply chains bypass Hormuz).

chain.l: Fatty acid derivatives · surface actives · biodiesel

cyclePos.verdict: At the top of the 42-month range. Soybean oil fell sharply through 2023-24 as biofuel mandates paused and demand softened, then reversed strongly through 2025-26 as biodiesel demand accelerated. The most recent May 2026 value is the 42-month high — unlike many other commodities in this library, the rise is not primarily war-driven.

soybean-oil.seasonNote: Some seasonality tied to Southern Hemisphere (Brazil) soybean harvest cycle (Feb-May) and US harvest (Oct-Dec). Biodiesel demand adds a northern winter heating-oil substitution effect.
soybean-oil.volNote: Moderate-to-high volatility — soybean oil is exposed to both agricultural (weather, harvest) and energy (biodiesel mandate) cycles simultaneously, creating two independent volatility sources.
soybean-oil.dyn3m: Soybean oil has risen sharply through early 2026, with May 2026 ($1,615.92/mt) the highest level in the 42-month window. The driver is biodiesel/renewable diesel demand in the US (Inflation Reduction Act biofuel tax credits) rather than food demand or the Iran war.

signals3m.text: Biodiesel / renewable diesel demand is the primary driver — not the Iran war; supply routes bypass Hormuz
May 2026 ($1,615/mt) is the 42-month high — structurally elevated, not a war premium

soybean-oil.dyn24m: Soybean oil fell from ~$1,381/mt in Jan 2023 to a trough of ~$903/mt in Dec 2024 as post-2022 food inflation reversed, then rose strongly through 2025-26 as US biodiesel demand surged under IRA tax credit policy.

signals24m.text: 2023-24: Sharp decline from $1,381 to $903 — post-2022 food price normalisation
2025-26: Strong recovery to $1,616 — US biodiesel/renewable diesel demand (IRA tax credits)

soybean-oil.upstreamNote: The IRA (Inflation Reduction Act) biofuel tax credits have created a structural demand floor for soybean oil in the US that is independent of food demand and geopolitics. This is a key difference from Corn and Wheat in this library.
soybean-oil.producersNote: The US crushing/refining industry is highly concentrated (Big Three: ADM, Bunge, Cargill) but price is ultimately set by CBOT futures and is globally competitive.

negPointers.body: Unlike most price increases in this library (war premium, gas cost), the soybean oil appreciation since 2024 is driven by US biofuel policy (IRA tax credits). This makes it more durable — it will not unwind quickly with a ceasefire. The negotiation leverage question is whether the specific supplier's formulation actually requires soy-origin inputs, or whether palm oil substitution is feasible.

negPointers.title: Palm oil substitution — check whether your formula uses CPO or soy oil
negPointers.body: Soybean oil and palm oil (CPO, tracked in this library) are partial substitutes in many formulations. CPO has also risen but from different drivers. If the supplier can switch to palm, the soy oil premium may not pass through fully to your formula cost.

corn.name: Corn (Maize)

regLabels.multi: Global — Corn FOB US Gulf (IMF/FRED PMAIZMTUSDM, $/mt)

corn.chainNote: Corn (Maize) is a primary feedstock for glucose, sorbitol, starch-derived chemicals, and some fermentation-based specialty ingredients. It is also the dominant livestock feed grain. Corn prices have fallen sharply since 2023 — down 29% from the January 2023 base — as the 2022 Ukraine war supply disruption unwound and record global harvests brought prices to multi-year lows. The Iran war had minimal direct effect on corn pricing.

cyclePos.verdict: Near the lower end of the 42-month range, with May 2026 ($215.62/mt) near multi-year lows. Corn has been one of the most clearly bearish agricultural stories since 2022 — the Ukraine-war supply disruption has fully unwound and global production has been strong. Buyer leverage is strong on corn-derived formula inputs.

corn.seasonNote: Strong seasonality — corn typically peaks in Q1 ahead of Southern Hemisphere harvest, troughs in Q3-Q4 as US and European harvests arrive. The seasonal low (Jul-Sep) is the best timing for corn-linked input renegotiation.
corn.volNote: Moderate-to-high volatility — corn is highly weather-sensitive (US Corn Belt drought is the classic shock) and geopolitically sensitive (Ukraine is a major exporter). The 2022 war shock and subsequent unwind is the dominant story of this 42-month window.
corn.dyn3m: Corn has been broadly stable and slightly rising in early 2026 ($203-216/mt), essentially flat. No Iran war effect — corn supply routes from the US, Brazil, Argentina, and Ukraine bypass the Strait of Hormuz entirely.

NA.name: Natural Gas — Henry Hub (NA)
NA.chainNote: Henry Hub is the US benchmark for natural gas. It matters for formula cost models primarily through the ammonia/nitrogen chain (gas = 70–80% of ammonia cash cost) and as a direct input to US chemical plant energy costs. Critically, Henry Hub is structurally insulated from the 2026 Iran war — the US is a domestic gas market with limited import exposure, and LNG export terminal capacity limits how much Persian Gulf disruptions can feed back into US prices. The January 2026 spike ($7.72/MMBtu) was a domestic cold weather event, not war-related; by Feb–May 2026, Henry Hub fell back sharply as weather normalised.

cyclePos.verdict: Mid-range after extraordinary volatility. The Jan 2026 spike (to 236 base-100) was a domestic weather event, not Iran war-related, and reversed completely by Feb–May 2026. Current level (-10% vs Jan 2023 base) reflects a US gas market that is fundamentally well-supplied and insulated from global LNG disruption.

NA.seasonNote: Strong seasonal pattern — Henry Hub peaks in winter (heating demand) and has a secondary summer peak (power generation / cooling). The January spike each year is partly seasonal; the Jan 2026 spike was seasonality amplified by an unusual cold wave.
NA.volNote: Very high volatility — the highest of any index in this library. US gas prices are driven by weather extremes and domestic supply/demand balance; single-month moves of 50–100%+ are historically common.
NA.dyn3m: Henry Hub spiked dramatically in January 2026 ($7.72/MMBtu, +136% vs the previous month) due to a severe US cold wave, then collapsed back to near-normal levels by February–May. This was entirely a weather event unrelated to the Iran war. EU gas (TTF) showed the opposite pattern — less seasonal volatility but a genuine war-driven spike in March 2026.

The spike was less severe than Europe's TTF because Japan has longer-term LNG contracts that buffered spot exposure. Unlike Henry Hub (which did not spike), Japan LNG did feel the war effect.

This structural advantage makes MEA chemical manufacturing (especially ammonia, methanol, and fertilisers) highly competitive globally. However, the 2026 Iran war disrupted MEA gas supply chains and created upward pressure even on domestic subsidised prices, particularly in smaller non-producing MEA economies. Global.name: Brent Crude Oil
Global.chainNote: Brent crude is the most widely-used global oil benchmark. It is the root upstream driver for the entire oil-derived cost chain in this library: naphtha → aromatics/olefins → HDPE/PP/base oil/LAB. The 2026 Iran war (Strait of Hormuz closure from 28 Feb 2026) caused Brent to surge from ~$62/bbl in late 2025 to a peak of $117.29/bbl in April 2026 — a +88% move in four months. By May 2026, it had retraced to ~$107/bbl on ceasefire progress, and by late June 2026 further to ~$73–74/bbl as shipping through the Strait resumed. The monthly average shown here lags the current spot.

guar-gum.name: Guar Gum (NCDEX futures)

regLabels.multi: India — NCDEX Guar Gum (GUARGUM5) futures

guar-gum.chainNote: Guar gum is a galactomannan polysaccharide extracted from guar beans (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba), grown almost exclusively in Rajasthan and Gujarat, India. Three distinct end markets drive demand: oil & gas hydraulic fracturing (historically the dominant swing factor — the 2012 speculative spike is canonical), food & pharmaceutical thickening/stabilisation, and mining flotation depression. The NCDEX GUARGUM5 contract is the global price reference.

chain.l: Mining reagent / food thickener / fracking fluid

cyclePos.verdict: At the top of its 42-month range — prices have risen steadily since the Feb 2025 reversal, driven by harvest inventory depletion and resumed oil & gas fracking demand. Current levels are the highest since Jan 2023.

guar-gum.seasonNote: Prices typically soften post-harvest (Oct–Dec) as new crop supply enters, then firm through H1 as stocks draw down. Oil & gas fracking demand (US shale, primarily H1–Q3) overlays this agricultural cycle.
guar-gum.volNote: Moderate volatility — lower than the 2012 speculative era, but the Feb–Mar 2025 reversal (+60% in 3 months) shows supply-side shocks can still be sharp.
guar-gum.dyn3m: Guar gum has continued its post-Feb 2025 recovery through H1 2026. The combination of tight Rajasthan/Gujarat harvests and resumed US shale fracking demand has sustained upward pressure. NCDEX GUARGUM5 futures currently around ₹11,531/5-quintal — the highest in over two years. Export demand from the US and Middle East oil & gas sector remains the primary driver.

signals3m.text: Oil & gas fracking demand resumed — US shale activity recovery pulling guar derivative orders higher.
Rajasthan/Gujarat harvest tightness — 2024 monsoon patterns left below-average carry-forward stocks.
+19% YoY — NCDEX 12-month change +19.12%, driven by supply depletion and export demand recovery.

guar-gum.outlook: The Indian Meteorological Department’s 2026 monsoon forecast will be the next major supply signal — a below-normal monsoon would extend the rally, while a strong harvest could ease prices by Q4 2026. Oil & gas fracking demand is the structural demand driver.
guar-gum.dyn24m: A full cycle visible in this window: 2023 Q4 decline on falling carry-forward stocks → 2024 mixed (Q1 oversupply dip, Q2 supply constriction, H2 bearish on weak EU demand) → Jan 2025 continued bearish (index trough at 76) → Feb 2025 sharp reversal begins (harvest inventory depletion, export demand) → Mar 2025 sharp acceleration (oil & gas fracking resumed, food processing steady) → H2 2025 continued moderate rise → 2026 continuation to current highs. India (Rajasthan/Gujarat) supplies the overwhelming majority of world guar gum — there is no meaningful diversification option.

signals24m.text: India supply monopoly — Rajasthan/Gujarat account for the vast majority of global guar production. No credible alternative source exists.
Oil & gas demand cyclicality — the 2024 H2 bearishness coincided with weak US shale spending; the 2025 reversal coincides with its recovery.
2024 trough at index 76 — a 24% decline from Jan 2023 base, driven by oversupply and weak EU demand.

guar-gum.upstreamNote: Supply is entirely monsoon-dependent; demand is split across three uncorrelated end markets (oil & gas, food, mining).
guar-gum.producersNote: Production is concentrated among a handful of Rajasthan-based processors. The market is fragmented below the top tier, with many small operators.
